# How to use the task catalog

This page is for a reader who wants to do something with the task catalog: find the
task in an experiment, read its model, compare two tasks, tag a dataset, or propose a
change. [The task model](task_model.md) explains the terms used here.

## Finding a task

Four routes lead to a task page.

- **By name or alias.** The search box in the sidebar indexes canonical names, aliases,
  definitions and variant names, so "CWIT", "Stroop" and "color-word interference"
  all reach the Stroop Color-Word Task.
- **By the kind of game.** [Tasks by game type](tasks/by_game_type.md) lists the
  {{ n_tasks }} tasks under the ten game types, and
  [tasks by facet](tasks/by_facet.md) lists, for each facet value, the tasks and
  variants that carry it.
- **By family.** The [task index](tasks/index.md) groups the tasks into task families
  such as conflict and interference tasks, span tasks and economic games. Each family
  has a scope sentence and a table of its tasks.
- **By process.** Each entry on a [process category page](processes/index.md) lists the
  tasks linked to the process, and the [task-process links](task_process_links.md) page
  gives the whole matrix.

The [alphabetical list](tasks/tasks_alphabetically.md) is the fallback when you know the
name but not the family.

## Reading a task page

Take the [Stroop Color-Word Task](tasks/hedtsk_stroop_color_word.md) as the example.

**Identifier and aliases.** The identifier `hedtsk_stroop_color_word` is the value to
record when tagging. The aliases are the other names the literature uses for the same
procedure.

**Game model.** The standard form of the task as a game, in the five parts of
[the task model](task_model.md): the game type, the game rules it states, the game
motivators, the game phases and the game facets, followed by the settings studies vary,
the material, and any combined game. Each value links to its definition on the
[game vocabulary](tasks/vocabulary.md) page. A rule the block does not list takes the
default of the game type.

**Inclusion test.** The three lists decide whether a particular experiment is an
instance of this task:

- *Procedure*, as ordered steps: color words (RED, BLUE) are printed in incongruent ink
  colors; participants name the ink color while ignoring the word.
- *Manipulations*, one variable per item: congruency (congruent, incongruent, neutral);
  proportion congruent; response modality (vocal, manual); stimulus type (classic,
  spatial, numerical).
- *Measurements*, one measure per item: Stroop interference effect (incongruent minus
  congruent RT); facilitation (neutral minus congruent); error rate; conflict adaptation
  (Gratton effect).

An experiment is an instance when its procedure matches, it manipulates at least one of
the listed variables, and it records at least one of the listed measures. If the
procedure does not match, it is a different task even if the construct is the same. If
the procedure matches but the experiment differs in a way listed under *Variants*, it
is an instance of that variant.

**Variants.** Each row names another form of the task that studies use, says what
differs from the standard form in the terms of the game model, lists the processes it
adds, and describes it in a note. Variants have identifiers of the form
`hedvar_<task>__<variant>`, so a dataset can be tagged with a variant when the
distinction matters. Things that are deliberately *not* variants, such as adding a
recording modality or testing a different population, are listed in the
[task criteria](methods/task_criteria/04_task_facets_and_variants.md).

**Cognitive processes.** The processes the task is hypothesized to engage, each linked
to its definition. These are the process tags a dataset using this task would carry.

**References.** *Key references* established the paradigm; *recent references* are
reviews or influential recent papers. Citations are reproduced as the source supplies
them.

**External links.** The corresponding Cognitive Atlas entry, with a qualifier when the
match is close rather than exact.

## Comparing two tasks

Open the two task pages and read their game models side by side, part by part. Start
with the game type: tasks of different types are different kinds of game, and the rest
of the comparison is between their motivators and facets. For tasks of the same type,
the game rules each one states are what separates them.
[Comparing tasks](task_model.md#comparing-tasks) on the task model page works through
an example.

## Reading a process page

Processes are presented one category to a page. The category page opens with the
category's scope, what is out of scope and any open issue about its boundaries. Each
process entry then gives the identifier, aliases with a note on the terminological
distinction, the definition, the tasks linked to it, and references. A process with no
linked tasks says so; it is kept because a task that engages it may be added.

## Tagging a dataset

The identifiers are stable enough to record now, even though how they will be expressed
in HED annotations and dataset metadata is still being decided. For a dataset:

1. Identify the task with the inclusion test, and the variant if one applies.
2. Record the task identifier (`hedtsk_...`) and, if applicable, the variant
   identifier (`hedvar_...`).
3. Record the process identifiers (`hed_...`) listed on the task page. Add processes
   the task page does not list only if the experiment's own design targets them; the
   task page lists what the paradigm is designed to probe, not everything it touches.
4. If the experiment is a task the catalog does not have, or a variant a task page
   does not list, model it (next section) and propose it rather than forcing a fit.

Resting runs, fixation blocks and questionnaire blocks are tagged the same way:
`hedtsk_rest` (eyes open or closed is one of its manipulations), `hedtsk_fixate`, or
`hedtsk_take_questionnaire`, with the processes their pages list. Feedback has no task
identifier of its own; it is an event of the task it belongs to, tagged
`Task-event-role/Feedback`.

## Modeling the task in a paper

A task that is described in a paper, whether or not the catalog has it, can be modeled
in the same terms by filling in the paper template.
[The modeling process](modeling_process.md) gives the steps and describes the template,
which is in the repository under `data/paper_models/`.

## Proposing a change

The task models are developed continuously and depend on their users to grow. The
repository's
[contributing guide](https://github.com/hed-standard/hed-task/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)
describes the process; in short, open an issue at
<https://github.com/hed-standard/hed-task/issues/new/choose>. There is a form for each
of the first three kinds below and for a correction, asking for the fields that are
needed; anything else goes in a blank issue.

- **A new task.** Give the canonical name and aliases, the procedure as ordered steps,
  the manipulations and the measurements in the form the inclusion tests use, the
  processes it engages, and one or two references. Say why it is not a variant of an
  existing task. A filled-in paper template is the most useful form.
- **A new variant.** Name the parent task, say how it differs from the standard form
  (which game rule, motivator, phase or facet), and say why that is not one of the
  excluded kinds of change (measurement modality, analysis, population, stimulus swap,
  and so on).
- **A new process.** Say when in a trial it happens, what elicits it, how it is
  measured, and which category it belongs in. Say why it is not an alias of an existing
  process.
- **A correction.** Anything wrong on a page: a definition, a game model, a reference,
  a link, a family assignment, an Atlas mapping. Quote the page and the text.
- **A disagreement with the model or a rule.** The task model and the criteria pages
  state things as they stand; arguments for changing them are welcome, and so are
  values the game vocabulary lacks.

The source for the site is at <https://github.com/hed-standard/hed-task>. The task and
process pages are generated from the data, so corrections are applied to the data, not
to the pages.
